CARDIAC CYCLE
Introduction
The cardiac cycle is divided into two main phases:
- period of ventricular contraction and blood ejection: systole
- period of ventricular relaxation and blood filling: diastole
At a heart rate of 72 beats/min, each cardiac cycle
lasts approximately 0.8 s with 0.3 s for systole and 0.5 s for diastole.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Systole
Systole is subdivided into two periods:
- period of isovolumetric ventricular contraction
- ventricular ejection period
CARDIAC CYCLE
Systole
1- Period of isovolumetric ventricular contraction
It represents the first part of systole where the ventricles
contract, all the heart valves are closed and the blood does not
can be ejected.
The ventricular volume therefore remains constant and the muscle develops a
tension but does not shorten.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Systole
2- Ventricular ejection period
When the pressure in the ventricles exceeds that of the aorta and trunk
pulmonary, the aortic and pulmonary valves open at the beginning of the period
ventricular ejection. Contracted ventricular muscle fibers
expel blood from the ventricles towards the aorta and the pulmonary trunk.
The volume of blood ejected from each ventricle is called ejection volume.
(VES).
CARDIAC CYCLE
Diastole
Diastole is subdivided into two periods:
- isovolumetric ventricular relaxation period
- ventricular filling period
CARDIAC CYCLE
Diastole
1- Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation period
The ventricles relax and the aortic and pulmonary valves
close. The atrioventricular (AV) valves are also closed.
The ventricular volume remains constant.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Diastole
2- Ventricular filling period
Opening of the AV valves causes ventricular filling to begin
with blood from the atria. Atrial contraction occurs in
end of diastole when ventricular filling is almost complete
(80% of filling).

CARDIAC CYCLE
1- The left atrium and ventricle are relaxed with a slight increase in atrial pressure.
2- The AV valve is open allowing blood to pass from the atrium to the ventricle.
3-4- The aortic valve remains closed throughout diastole because the aortic pressure is higher than the ventricular pressure, but tends to decrease during diastole.
CARDIAC CYCLE5- The arrival of blood from the atrium into the ventricle causes a slight increase in ventricular pressure, resulting in an increase in ventricular volume.
6- At the end of diastole, the sinus node discharges, resulting in depolarization of the atrium and appearance of the P wave on the ECG.
7- 8- The resulting contraction of the atrium causes an increase in atrial pressure with the passage of a small additional volume of blood into the ventricle.
9- At the end of ventricular diastole, the volume of blood in the ventricle constitutes the maximum volume that the latter can contain. It is called end-diastolic volume (EDV)

2- Ventricular systole
The ventricle, which until then had been relaxed during its filling, begins
to contract immediately after atrial contraction.
CARDIAC CYCLE
10- The depolarization wave passes into the ventricle through the atrioventricular node and propagates there, hence the appearance of the QRS complex on the ECG. The ventricle contracts.
11- This ventricular contraction leads to a very rapid and immediate increase in ventricular pressure exceeding atrial pressure.

12- The AV valve then closes. 13- The aortic pressure remains higher than the ventricular pressure, the aortic valve remains closed. The ventricle cannot empty: all the valves are closed. This is the phase of isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

19- Peak ventricular and aortic pressure are reached before the end of ventricular ejection.
20-21- In the last part of systole, the force of ventricular contraction decreases leading to a drop in blood ejection speed, resulting in a drop in aortic volume and pressure.

3- Protodiastole: isovolumetric relaxation
The diastole phase begins with the relaxation of the ventricular muscle and
the end of the ejection.
CARDIAC CYCLE
22- The appearance of the T wave on the ECG corresponds to the triggering of ventricular repolarization.

23- During ventricular relaxation, the ventricular pressure falls below the aortic pressure which remains significantly elevated with closure of the aortic valve. Blood bouncing against the valve causes a drop and then a rebound in aortic pressure, giving an appearance called a dicrotic notch.
24- The aortic and AV valves being closed, this is the isovolumetric ventricular relaxation phase
CARDIAC CYCLE
25- The isovolumetric ventricular relaxation phase ends with a drop in ventricular pressure below the atrial pressure.
26-27- The AV valve opens with blood flowing from the atrium to the ventricle.
28- The speed of blood flow is increased at the initial phase of filling by a rapid drop in ventricular pressure.

Left ventricular pressure-volume curve
CARDIAC CYCLE
Left ventricular pressure-volume curve
The cycle of the left ventricle can be represented on a diagram
pressure-volume.
At the beginning of systole, the mitral valve is closed, the pressure increases
without changes in volume: this is isovolumetric contraction. When
ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aorta, the aortic valve
opens: this is the ejection phase.
During rapid ejection, the volume decreases while the pressure
increase. During slow ejection, the volume continues to decrease and the
pressure decreases.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Left ventricular pressure-volume curve
When the ventricular pressure becomes lower than the pressure in
the aorta, the aortic valve closes.
Ventricular pressure continues to decrease while volume does not change
step: this is the isovolumetric relaxation phase.
The mitral valve then opens with a rapid increase in volume.

CARDIAC CYCLE
Left ventricular pressure-volume curve
The surface enclosed by the pressure-volume loop is equal to the work
carried out by the ventricle to eject blood into the aorta.

Pulmonary circulation pressures
Changes in pressure of the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries
are similar to those of the left ventricle and aorta, but
quantitatively, they are different.

Pulmonary circulation pressures
The pulmonary circulation is a low pressure system. The wall of
right ventricle is thinner than that of the left ventricle but the volumes
ejection of the two ventricles are identical.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Heart sounds
With a stethoscope, we hear two heart sounds due to closure
valves.
- B1: first heart sound, low tone, relatively long,
accompanying the closure of the AV valves, at the beginning of systole.
- B2: second heart sound, more intense, dry and rapid, due to closure
of the pulmonary and aortic valves, at the start of diastole.
CARDIAC CYCLE
Heart sounds
There are other noises called hissing that can be signs of
heart disease. They are induced by cardiac abnormalities at the origin
turbulent blood flow.
This flow turbulence may be due to rapid flow of blood into
the usual direction through an abnormally narrow valve: stenosis,
or by retrograde flow through a damaged valve and not
waterproof: insufficiency.
